audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for child sacrifice language, plural worship, siege, Elath population displacement, vassal language, sacred-treasury tribute, Damascus conquest and deportation, foreign altar copying, priestly compliance, temple reconfiguration, and imperial accommodation.

verses.restored: In seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham king of Judah became king.
Twenty years old was Ahaz when he became king, and sixteen years he reigned in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in eyes of YHWH his Divine, like David his father.
He walked in way of kings of Israel and even made his son pass through fire, according to abominations of nations whom YHWH dispossessed from before children of Israel.
He sacrificed and burned incense at high places, on hills, and under every green tree.
Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel went up to Jerusalem for war. They besieged Ahaz but were unable to overcome him.
At that time Rezin king of Aram restored Elath to Aram and drove Judeans from Elath; Arameans/Edomites came to Elath and lived there to this day.
Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, Your servant and your son am I. Come up and save me from hand of king of Aram and hand of king of Israel, who rise against me.
Ahaz took silver and gold found in house of YHWH and treasuries of king's house and sent a gift to king of Assyria.
King of Assyria listened to him. King of Assyria went up against Damascus, captured it, exiled its people to Kir, and put Rezin to death.
King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria and saw altar in Damascus. King Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest likeness of altar and its pattern according to all its workmanship.
Urijah the priest built altar according to all king Ahaz sent from Damascus; thus Urijah the priest made it before king Ahaz returned from Damascus.
King came from Damascus, saw altar, approached altar, and offered upon it.
He sent up his burnt offering and grain offering, poured his drink offering, and dashed blood of his peace offerings upon altar.
Bronze altar that was before YHWH he brought from front of house, from between new altar and house of YHWH, and placed it on north side of new altar.

King Ahaz commanded Urijah the priest, saying, Upon great altar send up morning burnt offering, evening grain offering, king's burnt offering and grain offering, burnt offering of all people of land, their grain offering and drink offerings; all blood of burnt offering and sacrifice you shall dash upon it. Bronze altar shall be for me to inquire/consider.
Urijah the priest did according to all king Ahaz commanded.
King Ahaz cut off panels of stands and removed basins from upon them; he took sea down from bronze cattle beneath it and placed it upon pavement of stones.
Covered Sabbath structure they built in house and outer entrance of king he turned from house of YHWH because of king of Assyria.
Remaining acts of Ahaz that he did, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Judah?
Ahaz lay with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in city of David. Hezekiah his son became king in his place.

translation_notes: Making a child 'pass through fire' is child endangerment or sacrifice and must be treated as abuse, not spiritual devotion, parental right, or cultural curiosity.
The nations named in polemical comparison must not become targets of ethnic contempt. Ahaz remains responsible for his own choices.
The siege by Aram and Israel threatens Jerusalem, while Elath's population is displaced and replaced. Territorial changes contain human removal, not only royal maps.

Ahaz calls himself Assyria's servant and son and pays with temple and palace treasure. The alliance relieves one threat by deepening imperial dependence and enabling Damascus's conquest and deportation.
Damascus's people are exiled to Kir and Rezin is executed. Judah's rescue is purchased through another population's suffering.
Copying a foreign altar is not inherently wrong because it is foreign; the ethical questions concern royal power, coercion, resource use, and the redirection of public worship.
Urijah complies with royal instructions before Ahaz returns. Priestly obedience to a ruler is not automatically faithfulness and does not erase institutional responsibility.

Temple objects are altered for imperial accommodation. Sacred traditions can be reorganized under political pressure, and no later reader should turn this into hostility toward artistic or interfaith exchange.
Chronology, the Elath reading, and the function of the bronze altar require textual and historical audit.
safety_note: Do not normalize child sacrifice, demonize foreign peoples or religious art, excuse priestly compliance with coercive power, or treat Assyrian intervention as clean rescue. Center the child, displaced Elath residents, deported Damascenes, and the way frightened rulers can trade communal treasure and institutional independence for imperial protection.
